title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array — binary search checking which half is sorted.
shortTitle: Search in Rotated Sorted Array — Binary Search Checking Which Half Is Sorted
topicTitle: Maximum Subarray / Kadane's Algorithm — running sum, reset w

s1_definition.profdef: Search in Rotated Sorted Array finds the index of a target value in a sorted array that has been rotated at one pivot. Because one half around the middle is always properly sorted, binary search determines which half is sorted, checks whether the target lies within that sorted half's range, and discards the other half. It locates the target, or reports absence, in logarithmic time with constant space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has rotated interest-rate checkpoints and an auditor needs to find the exact position of a specific rate. Looking at the middle checkpoint, the auditor notices that one side of it is still in perfect ascending order. If the target rate falls inside that orderly side's range, search there; otherwise the target must be on the messy side, so search there instead. Each look halves the remaining checkpoints.
s1_definition.oneliner: One half around the middle is always sorted, so check if the target fits in it and keep that half.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Search in Rotated Sorted Array finds the index of a target value in a sorted array that has been rotated at one pivot. Because one half around the middle is always properly sorted, binary search determines which half is sorted, checks whether the target lies within that sorted half's range, and discards the other half. It locates the target, or reports absence, in logarithmic time with constant space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has rotated interest-rate checkpoints and an auditor needs to find the exact position of a specific rate. Looking at the middle checkpoint, the auditor notices that one side of it is still in perfect ascending order. If the target rate falls inside that orderly side's range, search there; otherwise the target must be on the messy side, so search there instead. Each look halves the remaining checkpoints.

**One line to remember:** One half around the middle is always sorted, so check if the target fits in it and keep that half.

sections.s2_technical:
A rotated sorted array, split at any middle index, always has at least one properly sorted half. The trick is to detect which half is sorted and then use the ordinary binary-search range check on that half, because inside a sorted half you can tell with a simple range comparison whether the target could be there.

You keep a left and right index. At each step you compute the middle. If the element at middle equals the target, you are done. Otherwise you decide which half is sorted by comparing the element at left to the element at middle. If the left element is less than or equal to the middle element, the left half is sorted. In that case, if the target is greater than or equal to the left element and strictly less than the middle element, the target lies in the sorted left half, so you move right to middle minus one; otherwise you move left to middle plus one. If instead the left element is greater than the middle element, the right half is sorted, and you do the symmetric check: if the target is strictly greater than the middle element and less than or equal to the right element, you move left to middle plus one; otherwise you move right to middle minus one.

Detecting the sorted half is what makes this correct. In a rotated array the pivot sits in exactly one half, and the other half is cleanly sorted. By always identifying the sorted half you can use a precise range test, and whatever half the target is not guaranteed to be in gets discarded. This keeps the logarithmic time of ordinary binary search despite the rotation.

A senior point is the boundary comparisons. Using less-than-or-equal at the left-element-to-middle comparison correctly treats a two-element window and the case where left equals middle. The target range checks use inclusive bounds on the sorted end and exclusive bounds on the middle, which prevents including the middle element twice since it was already checked for equality. Getting these inclusive and exclusive boundaries exactly right is where most buggy implementations fail.

Another senior point is duplicates. If values can repeat, the comparison of left to middle can be ambiguous when they are equal, and you resolve it by nudging the left pointer inward by one when left, middle, and right all tie, which keeps correctness at the cost of a linear worst case. For distinct values this is not needed. For money I compare with BigDecimal compareTo so exact decimal rates are matched and ordered correctly.

A small finance-domain example: `if(rates[lo].compareTo(rates[mid])<=0){ if(target>=rates[lo] && target<rates[mid]) hi=mid-1; else lo=mid+1; } else { ... }` finds the target's index in logarithmic time.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores interest-rate checkpoints that were ascending but got rotated when the cycle restarted, and an audit feature must find the exact index of a specific rate so it can reference the surrounding checkpoints. The list can be long and audits are frequent. Searching a rotated sorted array with binary search is exactly this.

This is exactly how Search in Rotated Sorted Array works in Java — detecting which half around the middle is sorted and keeping the half that could contain the target.

Problem 2 — Sometimes the target rate is not present and the feature must report absence cleanly rather than looping forever, and rates are exact BigDecimal values. This shows the not-found path and money precision.

What the code will do: a `RotatedSearch` with `indexOfRate(BigDecimal[] rates, BigDecimal target)` using binary search that checks which half is sorted, returning the index or minus one. The demo searches for a present and an absent rate.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the rotated checkpoints are `4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2`, and the first target is `0`.

Step 1: lo is zero, hi is six. The middle index is three, holding `7`, which is not the target `0`. We compare the left element `4` to the middle `7`; since `4` is less than or equal to `7`, the left half is sorted. Is the target `0` in the range from `4` up to but not including `7`? No, `0` is below `4`, so the target is in the messy right half and lo becomes four.

Step 2: lo is four, hi is six. The middle index is five, holding `1`, not the target. We compare the left element at index four, which is `0`, to the middle `1`; since `0` is less than or equal to `1`, the left half is sorted. Is the target `0` in the range from `0` up to but not including `1`? Yes, `0` is at least `0` and less than `1`, so hi becomes four.

Step 3: lo is four, hi is four. The middle index is four, holding `0`, which equals the target, so we return index four. The search touched three middles instead of scanning all seven.

Step 4: for the second target `3`, the same process runs but every range check excludes `3`, so the window keeps shrinking until lo passes hi, and the method returns minus one, correctly reporting that `3` is absent without any infinite loop.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T19:00:00Z INFO Found rate at index 4
2026-10-26T19:00:00Z INFO Index of rate 0 = 4
2026-10-26T19:00:00Z WARNING Rate 3 not found
2026-10-26T19:00:00Z INFO Index of rate 3 = -1
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]  target=0  lo=0 hi=6
    │
    ▼
  while lo<=hi: mid; if a[mid]==t return; else which half is sorted?
    │ mid3=7 ; left[4..7] sorted ; 0 not in [4,7) → lo=4
    │ mid5=1 ; left[0..1] sorted ; 0 in [0,1)    → hi=4
    │ mid4=0 == target → return 4
    ▼
  index = 4   (target 3 → -1 after window collapses)
    ▼
  Output: index of the rate, or -1 if absent
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Search in Rotated Sorted Array finds the index of a target in a sorted array that has been rotated at one pivot, and I solve it with binary search in logarithmic time and constant space. The key observation is that when you split a rotated array at any middle index, at least one half is always properly sorted, so at each step I detect which half is sorted and use a precise range test to decide whether the target lives there.

Concretely, if the left element is less than or equal to the middle, the left half is sorted, and I check whether the target is at least the left value and strictly below the middle; if so I keep the left half, otherwise the right. If the left is greater than the middle, the right half is sorted and I do the symmetric check against the middle and the right boundary. Identifying the sorted half is what lets ordinary range reasoning work despite the rotation.

The part that catches people is the inclusive and exclusive boundaries. I use inclusive bounds on the sorted end and exclusive bounds at the middle so the middle element, which I already tested for equality, is never considered twice, and I use less-than-or-equal when comparing left to middle so two-element windows resolve correctly. For distinct values that is enough; for duplicates I nudge the left pointer inward when left, middle, and right all tie, accepting a linear worst case. I compare with BigDecimal compareTo so exact rates match.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on rotated interest-rate checkpoints so an audit feature could find the exact index of a given rate, and report cleanly when a rate was absent, even over a long list. Explaining the which-half-is-sorted detection, the exact boundary conditions, and the not-found path shows the interviewer that I can implement a tricky binary-search variant correctly, which is precisely what this problem tests.
